ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) in Bangladesh—particularly three-wheeler auto-rickshaws—has increased pressure on the national grid amid limited charging infrastructure. This study aims to develop a decision-oriented framework for designing optimized, region-specific hybrid renewable energy systems (HRES) for EV charging stations (EVCS), aligning system optimization with planning levers including site prioritization, tariff/incentive implications, demand response (DR) operation, and investment screening. Deterministic simulations were conducted for four high-EV-penetration regions—Gazipur, Khulna, Cox's Bazar, and Bhola—using HOMER Grid to optimize PV–battery–grid and PV–wind–grid configurations, with Gazipur also including a PV–diesel–battery–grid case, under site-specific resource and charging-demand profiles. EV charging sessions are analyzed by vehicle type and location, integrating EV-specific parameters such as charging frequency and energy per session. Grid-interactive operation was assessed through peak shaving, demand charge reduction, and energy arbitrage, alongside DR simulations for incentive-based curtailment. Across the four regions, Net Present Cost (NPC) ranged from $87,404 to $267,869 and Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) varied between $0.0515/kWh and $0.0695/kWh, with Khulna yielding the most cost-effective results. Renewable-dominant configurations indicate higher CO2 offset potential, supporting decarbonization-oriented planning. DR simulations indicate peak grid demand reductions of 30–70% during high-tariff hours, with demand-reduction revenue via battery dispatch or renewable contribution. Favorable Payback Period (PP), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), and Return on Investment (ROI) indicate investment feasibility, while sensitivity analyses capture variations in charging frequency and electricity pricing. This study provides novel insights for planning clean, cost-effective, and grid-responsive EV charging infrastructure for policymakers, energy planners, and investors in Bangladesh.

ce:section.ce:para: The accelerated increase in the global population, in conjunction with advancements in society, has markedly heightened the demand for energy. At this time, fossil fuels, which are inherently unsustainable and pose significant environmental risks, fulfill a large share of this demand [1]. As a result, greenhouse gas emissions have continued to rise. In 2023, global greenhouse gas emissions reached approximately 57 GtCO2e [2]. The power sector was the largest contributor, accounting for 26% mainly due to coal-fired plants. Among these, the transportation sector, particularly road transport, plays a critical role. Global road transport significantly drives air pollution and climate change, consuming 64% of global oil, 27% of total energy, and producing about 23% of energy-related CO2 emissions, prompting governments worldwide to increasingly work toward transforming conventional transportation systems into green alternatives by promoting EVs, which offer significant socio-economic and environmental advantages [3]. According to projections from the International Energy Agency, the total number of EVs worldwide is expected to reach 145 million by 2030 [4]. In 2022, fully electric cars made up 80% of the passenger vehicle sales in Norway, positioning the country as a dominant player in the EV market. Other leading nations include Iceland, where EVs made up 41% of sales, Netherlands at 24%, the Sweden at 32% and China, which recorded 4.4 million EV sales, representing 22% of the market. Furthermore, Norway holds the global record for the highest EV market penetration per capita, with 86.2% of new car sales in 2021 consisting of electric vehicles [5]. In contrast, the estimated count of two- and three-wheelers in Asia stood at about 490 million in 2019, with an annual market valuation of US$ 126 billion, of which nearly 7% were electric. This reflects why Asia is considered the most significant region for two- and three-wheelers and is making substantial progress in the transition to electric vehicles. This movement started more than ten years ago, when electric two-wheelers, commonly with pedal assistance, received financial backing in major urban areas of China to mitigate air pollution [6]. The largest global markets for two- and three-wheelers (2/3Ws) are found in China, India, and the ASEAN countries. In 2023, sales reached 19 million units in India, 17 million in China, and 14 million in ASEAN. Key ASEAN markets like Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Thailand see significantly higher 2/3W sales compared to light-duty vehicles (LDVs). In India, there are 157 two- and three-wheelers per 1000 people, compared to just 35 passenger cars [7]. To sustain and accelerate this growth, large-scale adoption of EVs require rapid development of clean charging and refueling infrastructure for smooth integration into the transport sector [8]. Although grid-powered EVs are feasible in developed nations with clean and sufficient electricity supply, this solution may not be practical for developing countries with limited or carbon-intensive grid infrastructure [9]. Nevertheless, while EVs contribute to decarbonization, they can also strain power networks in countries such as Bangladesh, where increased charging demand burdens the national grid during peak hours [10]. For instance, accommodating the rapid growth of EVs in Bangladesh requires an additional 500 MW of electricity per day from the national grid [11]. This surge in energy demand can result in unexpected peak loads, straining the transmission and distribution network, which leads to voltage fluctuations, line losses, and potential grid instability. Therefore, this can trigger load shedding, raise safety concerns, and impose an economic burden on consumers through higher electricity tariffs [12]. To be more specific, this additional load may overload system components and shorten transformer lifespan, as current energy infrastructure is not designed to handle such increased demand [13]. Secondly, Widespread EV charging on a single phase can cause phase imbalance and lead to voltage dips and fluctuations at grid connection points [14]. Moreover, EV chargers, being DC devices requiring power conversion, generate harmonics that can increase total harmonic distortion (THD), which may stay below 1% initially but rises as more chargers are connected to the grid [15]. Additionally, due to their non-linear load nature, EVs draw large amounts of real power in short periods, causing instability in the overall power network [16]. Finally, a high penetration of EVs into the power grid demands substantial real power, leading to increased energy losses; when 60% of EVs are connected, power losses can rise by up to 40% even during off-peak hours [17]. For example, In Bangladesh's residential networks, 50% EV penetration may raise voltage violation risks by approximately 25%, resulting in more frequent undervoltage events and transformer overloads [18]. This added burden further strains an already limited supply, as Bangladesh's installed generation capacity is around 24,143 MW against a demand of 15,500 MW to 16,000 MW, yet actual production typically ranges between 14,000 MW and 14,500 MW, leaving a deficit of 1500 to 2000 MW [19]. Rural Electrification Board, the country's largest rural power distributor, currently receives approximately 25% less energy supply than its actual demand resulting in daily load shedding of five to 6 h in rural areas [20]. Shortage of energy supplies like these have resulted in loses about $3.3 billion annually roughly 1.5% of its GDP due to unreliable electricity across homes, offices, and industries, further highlighting the economic consequences of an overstressed power infrastructure [21]. A clear example of this impact can be seen at NZ Apparels Ltd. in Narayanganj, where frequent load shedding damages around 15 types of sophisticated machines and components, resulting in yearly losses of approximately Tk 48 lakh [22]. Similarly, power shortages have cut BSRM's daily rod production by 25–30%, despite a capacity of 5500 tones across two factories [23]. In the current energy landscape, gas dominates net energy generation, accounting for 12,384 MW of total output. Coal produces 7179 MW, HFO 5885 MW, HSD 290 MW, imported power 1160 MW, renewables 1580.32 MW, and captive power 2800 MW of the total production. Corresponding percentages are depicted in Fig. 1 [24].

On top of that, given the rising national demand, current gas reserves are projected to be depleted within the next 10 to 12 years, posing a significant challenge to energy sustainability [25]. This looming depletion is already reflected in recent production trends, between FY2020 and FY2024, gas production fell from 24,993 to 21,075 MMCF, widening the production-distribution gap from 3492 to 6479 MMCF. Despite over 95% electrification by 2021, rising demand driven by urbanization, industrial growth, and rural electrification has outpaced supply due to fuel shortages, aging infrastructure, and inefficiencies in generation and distribution further straining the grid [26]. This growing shortfall in domestic gas supply has forced the country to increase its reliance on imports, leading to the import of 19.32 billion cubic feet of LNG in March 2024 alone [27]. To meet rising energy demand, Bangladesh signed three 15-year LNG purchase agreements in 2023 with Qatar and Oman. Qatar will supply 1.5 MTPA from 2026 to 2040 at 12.65% of the three-month average Brent price plus $0.50/MMBtu, while Oman will supply 0.25–1.5 MTPA at 11.9% plus $0.40/MMBtu. However, such long-term dependence on LNG imports is economically unsustainable for Bangladesh [28]. All of these generation from fossil fuel have resulted in a staggering 111.88 million tons of CO2 emission in 2023, marking a deeply concerning environmental setback [29]. This level of emissions has resulted in Bangladesh ranking as the world's second most air-polluted country, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 167 [30]. Moreover, in Bangladesh's two largest cities, Dhaka and Chittagong, the traffic sector is also the primary source of key air pollutants dominating NOx and CO emissions in Dhaka, and primarily contributing to NOx emissions in Chittagong [31]. To address these challenges, integrating renewable energy sources with hybrid energy storage systems into EVCS infrastructure offers a sustainable solution ensuring reliable power supply, reducing operational costs, and mitigating grid stress, ultimately establishing EVCS as a viable alternative to conventional fuel stations [32]. For example, Tesla established solar city to produce solar energy that powers the charging of Tesla electric vehicles [33]. In this context, solar energy presents a particularly viable option for Bangladesh due to its abundant solar resources. With solar irradiance ranging from 4 to 6.5 kWh/m2 across 94% of the country's land area and an average of 6.5 h of daily sunlight, the country is well-positioned to harness solar power effectively [34]. In addition to solar resources, Bangladesh possesses considerable wind energy potential, with estimates by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) indicating a capacity of 30,000 MW. Over 20,000 square kilometers of land are deemed suitable for wind farms, featuring wind speeds between 5.75 and 7.75 m/s [35]. Despite Bangladesh's abundant renewable energy potential including solar and wind its CO2 emissions continue to rise, reaching 124.793 million tonnes in 2023, up from 124.078 million tonnes in 2022 [36]. In response to this upward emissions trend, by the year 2030, Bangladesh aims to decrease its greenhouse gas emissions by 89.47 million tons of CO2 equivalent, representing a reduction of 21.85% compared to a business-as-usual scenario [37]. Bangladesh is already making small strides toward this goal through its growing renewable energy sector with total installed capacity for renewable energy of 1580.24 MW, Fig. 2 includes the contributions from solar energy, which accounts for 1286.25 MW, followed by hydro power at 230 MW, wind energy at 62.9 MW, biogas at 0.69 MW, and biomass at 0.4 MW [38]. Among the 1286.25 MW of solar capacity, Bangladesh's top five commissioned solar plants—Beximco Gaibandha (275 MW), Mongla and Orion Khulna (134.3 MW each), Mymensingh (73 MW), and Manikganj (35 MW) highlight its growing renewable sector [39]. Parallelly, the 60 MW Cox's Bazar Wind Power Plant marks the country's largest wind energy project, diversifying the renewable mix [40]. However, these projects together merely represent 5.05% of the total renewable capacity of 1580.24 MW in Bangladesh [24].

Given that transport contributed 11.6 million tonnes of CO2 in 2023 (9% of total emissions), targeted mitigation strategies are now a national priority [41]. As a mitigation effort, Bangladesh's NDC outlines a goal to reduce 3.39 million tons of CO2 from road transport by 2030 through 30% EV adoption. Correspondingly, Dhaka North and South City Corporations plan to expand EV use, targeting 10% of private cars and 80% of public transport to be electric by 2030, increasing to 50% and 100% respectively by 2040 [42]. As a result, electric vehicles are now extensively utilized across various regions of Bangladesh. The primary forms of EVs in operation within the country consist of electric vans, easy bikes, electric rickshaws, and electric scooters as shown in Fig. 3 [43].

According to estimates from the Road Transport and Highways Division under the Ministry of Road Transport and Bridges, approximately 2 million electric two- and three-wheelers are currently in operation across the country [44]. To provide a clearer picture of this growth trend, the number of registered auto rickshaws in Bangladesh from 2010 to 2024, highlighting the steady increase in their adoption over the years is illustrated in Fig. 4 [45]. These vehicles are powered by 4-5 pieces of 12V 200A batteries and are priced between 2 lakhs to 6 lakhs BDT, depending on the design and capacity [46].

As electric vehicle adoption increases in Bangladesh, the country's electricity demand has grown by over 7% annually, with peak demand expected to surpass 38 GW by 2041 [47]. To support the growing number of these electric vehicles, dedicated charging infrastructure has been introduced across the country resulting, 15 solar charging stations, as detailed in Table 1, by May 2024, with a cumulative capacity of 0.291 MWp. Among these, the smallest station has a capacity of 8.5 kWp, while the largest reaches 30 kWp. The average capacity of the stations is estimated to be between 20 kWp and 21 kWp [48]. However, the current limited number of charging stations is insufficient to accommodate the anticipated surge in electric vehicles in the near future. Beyond their inadequate quantity, concerns also arise regarding the strategic placement and interoperability of these stations, which are critical for establishing a sustainable nationwide infrastructure.

Thus, to support EV users, several companies including BYD, Ekhon Charge, and Crack Platoon are working together to install charging stations across the country, strategically focusing on key locations like highways, tourist destinations, hotels, and commercial hubs [49].

Moreover, in Bangladesh to address broader environmental concerns such as air pollution and the need for affordable energy a comprehensive Electric Vehicle Charging Guideline has been introduced. This guideline is designed to encourage the creation of a charging network that ensures safety, trustworthy, and accessible, thereby stimulating the widespread adoption of electric vehicles and reducing reliance on fossil fuels. To maintain compatibility and efficiency at these public charging stations, electric vehicles can be charged with one or more of the chargers listed in Table 2, as approved by the Bangladesh government [50]. Which will encourage integrating electric vehicle charging into the grid resulting a significant 10% drop in grid operating costs, a 40% reduction in expenses associated with renewable energy curtailment, and a 30% decrease in charging price [51].

This study addresses critical gaps in HRES-based EVCS research by performing a multi-location analysis across four regions in Bangladesh with high EV penetration—Gazipur, Cox's Bazar, Khulna, and Bhola. It provides a comprehensive framework for optimizing the design of HRES-based EVCS, offering valuable insights to policymakers and stakeholders.

The research of [52] seeks to develop a grid-integrated HRES that accommodates residential and EV charging requirements during scheduled power outages in Bangladesh. By employing HOMER Pro software, the optimal arrangement of PV systems, wind energy and BS achieves a LCOE of $0.0714 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), an NPC of $1.82 million and an annual emission of 164,812 kg of CO2. The configuration includes a 2 kW wind turbine (WT), a 237 kW inverter, an 836 kWh BS and a 377 kW PV module. A HES combining wind energy, battery storage and PV technology has been proposed by the author for the purpose of supplying power to supermarkets in Morocco. Utilizing HOMER grid software for optimization, the design achieves a LCOE of $0.0841 per kWh, leading to a remarkable 71.66% reduction in operational costs, which translates to an annual expenditure of $0.124 million. The optimal configuration for the Dakhla site includes a 65 kW inverter, 107 kW of PV, 300 kW of wind generation, 107 kW of PV and 12 batteries [53]. A feedback-driven scheduling method for electric vehicles is presented, incorporating a multi-regional master-slave model and evolutionary game theory. It models real-time pricing in virtual power plants and optimizes EV charging behavior through evolutionary game dynamics with load correction. Simulation results show a 2.12% deviation in load response, a 24.6% reduction in EV charging costs, and significant revenue gains for operators [54]. The article referenced as [55] elaborates on a refined method for deploying BTS telecommunications systems in multiple regions of Pakistan, using Homer grid software. The LCOE for standalone hybrid systems is found to range from $0.1096 to $0.2325 per kWh. Conversely, on-grid hybrid systems present an average LCOE between $0.004065 and $0.03559 per kWh. The addition of0 EVCS, along with relevant incentives, has further diminished the average LCOE. The research conducted in this study emphasizes the swift expansion of electric autorickshaws, which poses a considerable challenge to the national power infrastructure of Bangladesh, consuming approximately 4660 MWh on a daily basis. This consumption starkly contrasts with the estimated monthly solar energy production of 23,000 MWh available within the same sector [56]. Researchers used HOMER Grid to assess the techno-economic impacts of home and fast EV charging based on user demographics. Home charging increases grid usage by 59.9% and raises NPC by 65.5%. Without solar PV, charging stations consume 60% more grid power and incur 58% higher NPC. The study also concludes with a set of policy recommendations [57]. This paper [58] details for Dhaka a waste management system is tailored, which capitalizes on waste valorization to produce bioenergy for EVCS and the national grid. The initiative involves the design of a biomass power plant, a thorough economic viability analysis, and an evaluation of its environmental impact, particularly in terms of CO2 emissions, conducted through HOMER Pro. A solar-powered, grid-connected EV charging station optimized using HOMER Grid is proposed for Tohana, Haryana. The system includes 928 kW of PV, 1 MWh of battery storage, and a 190 kW converter, achieving a COE of $0.130/kWh and a NPC of $1.10 million [59]. A research investigation assesses the techno-economic and environmental effectiveness of six hybrid energy systems (HESs) located in Kunder Char, Bangladesh, employing HOMER Pro software for analysis. Among the five off-grid and one on-grid technologies analyzed, the on-grid system proves to be the most economically viable, with a NPC of $1.43 million and a LCOE of $0.0436/kWh [60]. Additionally, the PV system produces 86,961,688 kWh/year, facilitating 363,899 charging sessions annually. Several other techno-economic analysis of hybrid energy systems are presented in [116], [117], [118], [119], [120], and [121]. The main features of these studies are shown in Table 3.

Despite significant progress in the integration of HRES into EVCS, several important gaps remain in the existing literature, particularly in the context of Bangladesh and similar emerging economies. One key gap is the lack of integration of EV-specific factors in energy system models. Most studies have relied on generalized load profiles, often treating EV charging demand as a conventional, steady electrical load. However, this simplification overlooks the dynamic nature of EV charging, including variations in charging times, vehicle battery capacities, vehicle-specific usage patterns, charger types, charging frequencies, and the detailed analysis of charging sessions for different vehicle types. This gap reduces the accuracy and reliability of system models, which are crucial for realistic system optimization and economic feasibility evaluations.

Another notable gap is the lack of multi-location studies, especially in regions with variable renewable resource availability, such as Bangladesh. Most existing research focuses on single-location analyses, which limits the applicability of findings to broader contexts with different geographic, climatic, and socioeconomic conditions. For example, studies conducted solely in urban areas might not account for the renewable resource potential or EV adoption rates in rural or coastal areas, which can differ significantly.

Additionally, the current literature often overlooks the financial implications, including the use of critical financial metrics such as payback period, internal rate of return, and return on investment in the context of renewable-powered EV charging. These are essential for policymakers and investors when evaluating the long-term sustainability of EVCS projects. A significant gap in the literature is the lack of sensitivity analysis regarding the variability in EV charging demand and charging price fluctuations. This gap limits the ability to fully assess the operational robustness of EVCS, as real-world systems are subject to dynamic changes in both demand and pricing, which can have substantial impacts on system performance and economic viability.

Moreover, current studies rarely incorporate grid interaction strategies such as DR modeling within EVCS-HRES frameworks. The role of DR in managing peak load, reducing grid dependency, and enhancing economic return—particularly under variable renewable generation—is underexplored, especially in the context of developing energy systems like Bangladesh.

By integrating EV-specific parameters and conducting a multi-location analysis, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge in HRES for EVCS and provides a more comprehensive framework for evaluating economic feasibility and system performance across regions with differing renewable resources and EV demand profiles.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Research gaps, study motivation, and objectives
ce:section.ce:para:
Table 3 presents a comparative evaluation of previous studies across various hybrid energy configurations, analytical approaches, and optimization criteria. The key insights from this review reveal several gaps that, if addressed, could significantly enhance the design, performance, and economic feasibility of future energy systems. These gaps are outlined below:➢
Research is largely region-specific in Bangladesh, with limited studies assessing hybrid systems in varying geographic and climatic conditions. Expanding the scope to diverse locations could improve adaptability.➢
Numerous studies overlook key financial metrics such as return on investment, payback period, and internal rate of return, which are crucial for policymakers, investors, and energy planners when considering the implementation of renewable-powered EVCS.➢
A significant portion of the research depends on HOMER Pro, which, while widely used for hybrid energy system analysis, lacks dedicated EV load modeling. As a result, EV loads are often approximated as conventional demand, reducing modeling accuracy.➢
In addition, a comprehensive performance evaluation of EVCS, including a thorough analysis of EV charging sessions for each system at each location, is lacking, resulting in a gap in understanding their actual operational efficiency.➢
Most existing studies do not incorporate grid interaction strategies such as DR, limiting insights into peak load management, grid reliability enhancement, and economic performance optimization in grid-connected HRES-EVCS.➢
Another key gap is the limited consideration of EV-specific parameters in sensitivity analyses, particularly variations in EV session and charging price, which remain largely unexamined.

Despite progress in HRES integration for EVCS, these gaps constrain the ability of the literature to support strategic decisions on EVCS deployment in emerging economies such as Bangladesh. This study is therefore motivated to provide a decision-oriented framework that links techno-economic optimization with practical strategy levers—including site prioritization, tariff/incentive implications, DR-oriented operation, and investment screening—for scalable, grid-responsive EV charging infrastructure.

This study contributes by improving the technical realism of HRES–EVCS modeling (through EV-specific charging behavior and session-based analysis) while translating results into decision-relevant evidence for energy strategy and policy-making in Bangladesh. In particular, the multi-location comparison across resource-diverse regions and the inclusion of DR-oriented operation provides practical guidance on EVCS siting priorities, tariff/incentive implications, DR program design for peak management, and investment decision support using feasibility indicators (e.g., PP/IRR/ROI)—all of which support clean-energy transition planning and distribution-side demand management.

The objectives below are framed to inform strategic decisions on EVCS deployment, charging tariff/incentive implications, and DR-oriented operation for peak reduction and improved project bankability. Accordingly, the objectives of this study are:1.
To conduct a multi-location assessment across Gazipur, Khulna, Cox's Bazar, and Bhola to capture regional variation in renewable resources and EV demand.2.
To integrate EV-specific charging parameters into energy system models to improve the accuracy and reliability of HRES for EVCS, considering dynamic charging demand, charger types, vehicle types, and charging sessions.3.
To quantify economic and investment feasibility using decision-relevant financial indicators (e.g., NPC, LCOE, PP, IRR, ROI) alongside key technical and environmental performance metrics.4.
To conduct a session-level operational performance assessment of the optimized EVCS at each study location by quantifying charging energy served, temporal charging patterns, peak demand/peak window behavior, and grid interactions (purchases/exports).5.
To evaluate grid-interaction and operational strategies, including demand-response-oriented operation (e.g., peak shaving, demand-limit management, time-based incentives), to assess implications for distribution-side planning.6.
To conduct sensitivity analysis on key uncertainties (e.g., charging demand intensity and charging price) to test robustness and identify conditions under which each configuration remains viable.7.
To derive actionable recommendations for Bangladesh's energy strategy (siting priorities, tariff/incentive implications, DR program design, and investment signals for EVCS deployment).

The objectives are evaluated using deterministic, planning-level simulations at an hourly time-step. Feeder-level power-flow constraints, network reinforcement planning, and vehicle to grid services are outside the scope of this work.

To address the gaps outlined in section 1.2, this study presents several novel contributions:✓
Unlike conventional HRES studies, which often approximate EV loads as conventional demand or ignore their fluctuating nature, this study incorporates a detailed, time-based EV load profile based on real-world usage patterns. By considering factors such as charging times, vehicle battery capacities, and the frequency of charging sessions, the model allows for more accurate simulations of the daily and monthly load profiles specific to three-wheeler EVs in Bangladesh, addressing the growing demand for sustainable charging infrastructure in high EV-penetration areas.✓
In this study, the modeling framework is extended to allow for the precise selection of EV charger types, the specification of charging prices, and the estimation of charging sessions per day. By integrating these dynamic parameters, energy demand is evaluated over different time scales, ranging from individual charging sessions to daily and monthly consumption. This enables a more realistic representation of EV charging behavior compared to conventional models, ensuring that the resulting system optimization is better aligned with real-world operational conditions. These enhancements, enabled by HOMER Grid, offer a more comprehensive and accurate framework for optimizing the design and economic viability of renewable-powered EVCS. HOMER Grid's advanced algorithm optimizes time-step-level energy allocation in EVCS systems. Unlike studies that primarily focus on component sizing, this work emphasizes operational strategies such as energy arbitrage, peak demand shaving, and dynamic grid demand limit adjustment.✓
This research expands the scope of HRES-based EVCS studies by conducting a multi-location analysis across four high-EV-penetration (3-wheeler) regions in Bangladesh—Gazipur, Cox's Bazar, Khulna, and Bhola. Unlike previous studies that primarily focus on a single site, this study offers a broader perspective on how regional differences in renewable energy availability and EV demand impact system performance.✓
A thorough techno-economic analysis is conducted, assessing system costs, energy savings, load demand, resource availability and financial metrics such as return on investment, payback period, and internal rate of return— factors often overlooked in existing literature. The PV/Battery/Grid hybrid energy system is identified as the most suitable option for designing EVCS in Gazipur and Khulna, while the PV/Wind/Grid system is preferred for Cox's Bazar and Bhola, offering optimized energy and NPCs. By incorporating both technical and economic perspectives, this research offers a well-rounded framework for the sustainable development of EVCS in Bangladesh.✓
The analysis also examines individual system components, including solar PV, wind turbine, battery state of charge, and grid integration.✓
Beyond general system-level assessments, this study provides a comprehensive performance evaluation of EVCS. It analyzes EV charging output at both daily and monthly scales, capturing fluctuations in power consumption, station efficiency, and grid interactions. This detailed performance review fills a critical research gap, offering a more accurate representation of real-world EVCS operation.✓
This study incorporates DR modeling across all system configurations to evaluate grid-interactive behavior. By simulating DR events with time-based incentives, the analysis quantifies peak load shaving, battery dispatch patterns, and financial returns—providing utility-relevant insights often overlooked in HRES-based EVCS studies.✓
A detailed sensitivity analysis is presented, systematically examining EV-specific factors such as variations in daily EV charging sessions and charging prices. Environmental factors, including solar radiation and wind speed, are also considered in the analysis. This novel approach ensures a more realistic and dynamic evaluation of EVCS operation under varying conditions, providing insights into how technical and environmental factors influence the feasibility of the system.✓
Translates the optimization results into planning-relevant insights for EVCS siting, tariff/incentive implications, DR-enabled operation, and investment screening in Bangladesh.

This paper analyzes renewable energy integration for EVCS in Bangladesh. Section 1 reviews literature, identifies gaps, and highlights contributions. Section 2 outlines the methodology, covering framework, optimization, site selection, and resource assessment (solar, wind), along with EV load estimation. Section 3 presents the system design, including modeling, specifications, and optimization criteria. Section 4 presents a thorough analysis of EV sessions, system optimization, energy balance, grid transactions, surplus energy, and cost breakdown. It also covers the performance of different energy sources, economic performance, emissions, detailed sensitivity analysis, policy implementation, and socio-economic impacts. Section 5 concludes with key findings, implications, and future directions.

The methodological framework presented in Fig. 5(a) outlines a Sequential approach adopted in this research. The study begins with a foundational analysis of EV technology, its practical applications, and its significance in the current energy landscape. A thorough literature review is conducted to identify research gaps and establish key objectives. The proposed hybrid system for EVCS is then evaluated from technical, economic, and environmental standpoints. By considering real-world energy demands and system constraints, the goal of this study is to create an optimized solution tailored for sustainable EV charging infrastructure. Following this, the feasibility of integrating renewable energy is assessed by analyzing resource availability and atmospheric conditions at the selected location. The study also examines the impact of scheduled EV charging and cumulative load demand. Key decision variables and optimization constraints are defined to guide system modeling. Each system component's technical attributes and governing equations are outlined for clarity. Additionally, economic parameters related to solar PV, wind energy, and storage systems are identified for optimization. The study incorporates diverse energy sources to ensure energy security and cost-effectiveness while minimizing dependence on fossil fuels. HOMER Grid software is utilized due to its ability to model diverse energy technologies, dedicated EV load modelling, cost factors, and renewable resource availability. The required parameters are input into the software, and optimization is carried out based on selected objective functions and constraints. HOMER's energy balance algorithm simulates system performance at each time interval, ensuring that energy generation aligns with demand and predefined constraints. This approach provides a comprehensive analysis of how different hybrid energy configurations perform under various operational conditions. The system configuration is designed based on projected load demand, with a focus on maximizing renewable energy utilization for EV charging. The optimal hybrid system is determined through load forecasting and performance analysis. The results present key metrics, including energy generation and consumption, EVCS performance, EV load consumption scenarios, cost estimations, and environmental impacts. To enhance model accuracy, sensitivity analyses are performed, identifying critical factors influencing system efficiency and economic viability.

HOMER Grid software is created by the United States National Renewable Energy Laboratory. This tool takes various inputs, including load profiles, renewable energy resource data (solar, wind), system components (solar PV, wind turbines, batteries, generators), grid electricity pricing, and economic parameters like capital costs and discount rates. It processes these inputs to simulate different system configurations and evaluates their performance. Optimization in HOMER Grid occurs through a simulation-based approach that evaluates multiple system configurations to determine the most cost-effective and technically feasible solution for a given energy system.

The optimization process of HOMER Grid software to evaluate and design HRESs is depicted in Fig. 5(b). The process begins with defining the input data and establishing model constraints. A set of hybridization scenarios is then generated to explore different configurations of renewable and conventional energy sources. Each scenario undergoes a feasibility check to ensure that it meets the required operational constraints. If a scenario is found to be infeasible, the process is iterated to the next scenario until all possible configurations are evaluated. For each feasible system, the optimization process is conducted to determine the optimal design based on techno-economic and environmental performance. The algorithm is used to evaluate energy generation, component sizing, and overall system performance. The results include cost metrics such as NPC and LCOE, environmental impact assessments through emissions data, and operational performance indicators like optimized system sizing, financial feasibility (PP, IRR, ROI), energy production breakdown, and grid dependency insights and renewable fraction (RF). If the precision criterion of NPC is not met, the system components are resized and re-evaluated to enhance system efficiency and cost-effectiveness. This repetitive process persists until an ideal balance is attained.

The EV section of HOMER Grid software allows users to input the number of vehicles across 24-h time slots to analyze the effect of charging load patterns. It also offers a selection of various car producers and their respective battery capacities for simulation. Additionally, HOMER Grid offers features to choose different charging station types, including Level 1 and Level 3 facilities. Users can adjust the power of charging points as needed and modify the number of charging points accordingly.

In this study, four strategic locations in Bangladesh—Gazipur, Cox's Bazar, Khulna, and Bhola—have been selected for the implementation of hybrid EVCS. These locations are chosen due to their high EV usage and significant renewable energy resource potential. Gazipur, located near the capital city Dhaka, has a rapidly increasing number of EVs due to its proximity to urban centers and the high demand for sustainable transportation option [122]. Correspondingly, Cox's Bazar, a prominent tourist destination, experiences a continuous influx of visitors throughout the year, which raises the need for sustainable EV charging solutions [11]. Khulna, one of Bangladesh's largest metropolitan areas, also has a growing EV population and is ideal for hybrid EVCS implementation due to its access to renewable resources [56]. Bhola, situated in the coastal zone, is especially favorable due to its wind and solar energy potential. Among the locations, only Gazipur has two solar-powered EVCS which is inadequate to meet the growing EV load [48]. Consequently, these sites have been selected to explore a sustainable and scalable solution for hybrid EVCS that optimally utilizes available renewable resources. Further details on the selected locations are presented in Table 4 [123–127], and site locations are displayed in Fig. 6.

Bangladesh has significant potential for renewable energy, particularly solar and wind power. With abundant sunlight throughout the year, solar energy is the most promising resource. Wind energy potential is highest in coastal regions while other regions have ample wind speed.

The solar resource data (monthly average solar irradiance and clearness index) for Gazipur, Cox's Bazar, Khulna, and Bhola is presented in Fig. 7. In Khulna, the daily radiation reaches a maximum value in April at 6.070 kWh/m2/day, which is the highest among all locations, and the lowest value is seen in July at 3.995 kWh/m2/day. For Bhola, the solar radiation peaks in April at 5.705 kWh/m2/day, while the lowest value is in July at 3.685 kWh/m2/day, which is the lowest among all four locations. Fig. 8 illustrates the average wind speed for each month values for Gazipur, Cox's Bazar, Khulna, and Bhola. The data is collected from NREL using Homer Grid [128]. ce:section.ce:section-title: Insight into the different categories of EV charging stations
ce:section.ce:para: In a rapidly evolving country like Bangladesh, a broad range of gasoline- and electric-powered two-, three-, and four-wheeled vehicles can be frequently observed on roads and highways [129]. Among these, three-wheeled modes of transport—such as auto-rickshaws, tom-toms, and easy bikes—play a particularly important role in suburban and rural mobility. Since their introduction in 2004, Electric Three-Wheelers (E3Ws) have experienced widespread adoption across the country, with an estimated one million currently in operation. These vehicles have become central to short-range and intra-city transportation, especially in key urban areas like Gazipur, where dense industrial zones exist alongside numerous governmental and non-governmental institutions, creating significant demand for public transport. Charging for EVs in Bangladesh often begins at the household level, commonly referred to as private charging. A typical residential setup uses a single-phase 230-V, 15-amp connection with a maximum output of around 2.5 kW. Most residential chargers can supply energy in the range of 11 kWh to 22 kWh [130]. The most widely adopted method is AC charging, which includes both Level 1 and Level 2 systems. Table 5 shows an overview of different types of EV chargers.

Level 1 charging operates on a standard 120-V, 16-amp input, using everyday household outlets. It can be utilized with the power cables provided with most EVs, making it easily accessible and cost-free in terms of installation. One of its main advantages is its low impact on peak power demand. However, it is also the slowest charging option; it typically takes 8 to 16 h to fully charge a battery using a 1.9 kW output [131], which makes it unsuitable for users with high daily usage or limited charging time. Level 2 charging involves a higher input voltage of 208 to 240 V and supports up to 80 amps, delivering power at rates of up to 19.2 kW [132]. This setup significantly reduces charging time, usually adding 10 to 20 miles of driving range per hour of charging, and is more energy-efficient than Level 1. Because of its faster performance, it is suitable for both residential and public use. However, its main drawback lies in the higher installation costs and the potential for increased electricity bills due to its greater energy demand. DC Fast Charging, or Level 3, provides a much faster alternative. These chargers operate at approximately 480 V, with power outputs ranging from 36 to 240 kW and charging voltages between 200 and 600 V [131]. They can charge an electric vehicle to 80% capacity in just 15 to 45 min [133]. This rapid charging time is highly beneficial for commercial settings and long-distance travel, saving both time and operational costs. However, these advantages come with trade-offs. Installation and maintenance costs for DC fast chargers are significantly higher, and their high-power input may cause faster battery wear over time [122].

EVs are becoming more common in Bangladesh. Especially City areas seeing a higher increase in EVs due to low operating costs and higher efficiency in stop-and-go traffic. In Bangladesh, the prevalent types of electric vehicles are electric scooters, easy bikes, electric vans, and electric rickshaws. To incorporate EV load profiles into the HOMER Grid model, a detailed approach was adopted by analyzing the EV characteristics and charging behavior specific to each region. A detailed description of those four types of EVs is presented in Table 6. This research considers 30 easy bikes, 40 electric rickshaws, 20 electric vans, and 10 electric scooters for Gazipur and for Cox's Bazar 25 electric rickshaws, 40 easy bikes, 10 electric vans, and 5 electric scooters is considered. Again, in Khulna, the study incorporates 30 easy bikes, 35 electric rickshaws, 15 electric vans, and 10 electric scooters. In conclusion, the analysis also incorporates a fleet of 30 electric bikes, 30 electric rickshaws, 10 electric vans, and 5 electric scooters in Bhola. Therefore, the total number of EVs considered for Gazipur, Cox's Bazar, Khulna and Bhola are 100, 80, 80 and 75, respectively. Those EVs are powered by batteries. As in the daytime, EVs are used for transporting passengers, so generally batteries are charged at night. The energy consumption per EV varies based on the type of vehicle.

Energy consumption of each EV type is calculated based on battery specifications typically used by the EV owners. Each EV generally uses 4 to 5 batteries connected in series. This results in a higher overall system voltage, which determines the total energy storage capacity. For instance, easy bikes generally use 60V, 160Ah lead-acid battery, resulting in an energy consumption of 9.6 kWh per full charge. Electric rickshaws commonly run on 48V, 80Ah batteries, equating to 3.84 kWh, while electric scooters often use 72V, 20Ah batteries, consuming 1.44 kWh of energy. Additionally, electric vans are equipped with 48V, 80Ah batteries, resulting in 3.84 kWh energy consumption upon full charge. These battery specifications are taken from manufacturer datasheets and local distributor documentation [134,138]. Using these values, energy consumption per vehicle type was calculated using the formula:
Energy demand/consumption (kWh) = (Battery Voltage × Battery Capacity in Ah)/1000.

These EVs lead to total daily energy usage of 532.8 kWh in Gazipur, 525.6 kWh in Cox's Bazar, 494.4 kWh in Khulna, 532.8 kWh in Gazipur, and 448.8 kWh in Bhola. Table 7 presents the proportion of EV population and approximate energy consumption for the selected locations. Fig. 9 depicts a visual representation of the daily charging profile of EVCS at the study sites. The graph indicates a gradual increase in load after the evening period, while the demand remains significantly lower from morning to afternoon. Moreover, at night, the EV load remains high due to the increased demand for charging, as most EVs are plugged in for overnight recharging. The annual load profile in Fig. 10 indicates that the demand for EVCS remains consistent throughout the year.

In HOMER Grid, these EV loads are treated as deferrable loads, allowing the optimization engine to schedule EV charging sessions based on system economics and constraints. The chosen charger type is the deferrable EV charger (Level 2). This type of charger provides flexibility in scheduling, allowing users to optimize the timing of EV charging sessions throughout the day, enabling more efficient energy management. Table 8 shows the average sessions per hour for four regions, distributed across 24 h, reflecting user behavior with clear overnight charging dominance (10:00 p.m.–5:00 a.m.), minimal activity during daytime hours when vehicles are in use, and a gradual rise in the evening as EVs return to base for recharging. HOMER Grid optimizes the scheduling of electric vehicles by dynamically allocating them to available time slots, ensuring that load distribution aligns with both technical and economic efficiency. For each defined session, a vehicle is randomly selected from the available EV population, with the exact arrival time of the vehicle being randomly assigned within the designated hour [139]. It prioritizes charging by focusing on tariff optimization or shifting EV charging to lower-cost hours, aligning charging sessions with surplus energy from renewable sources, managing battery storage conditions, and preventing grid overloads. It may delay or reschedule charging to avoid grid peak hours or make better use of midday solar output. For instance, an EV charging session defined for the early evening hours may be deferred to mid-afternoon if solar generation is at its peak and session flexibility allows. Such scheduling helps reduce system cost and improves the utilization of renewable energy resources. To further refine the realism of the simulation, HOMER Grid's EV load modeling interface was configured using detailed variability parameters. These included a mean charging session duration of 7 h, session duration variability of 10%, session energy variability of 20%, and day-to-day as well as timestep visit frequency variability set at 10% and 20%, respectively. These settings allowed HOMER Grid to stochastically alter charging times, session lengths, and energy per session, introducing the kind of behavioral uncertainty found in real-world EV charging. Rather than treating EV charging as a fixed, inflexible load, this approach enabled the model to reflect variation in arrival time, state of charge, and user preference.

While HOMER Grid is powerful in scheduling and prioritizing deferrable EV loads, it has some limitations. Notably, it does not account for battery degradation over time, which impacts the long-term performance and capacity of EVs. As EVs undergo repeated charging and discharging cycles, their capacity diminishes, which could affect charging efficiency and energy demand. Additionally, factors such as state of charge (SOC) upon arrival and user-specific charging preferences are not integrated into the model's charging pattern. The model also lacks the ability to simulate trip-based discharge or real-time SOC changes. Furthermore, HOMER Grid does not incorporate Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology, which allows EVs to return electricity to the grid when needed.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Renewable energy integration for EV charging stations
ce:section.ce:para: It is important to carefully examine the accessible power sources that can adequately satisfy the energy requirements of the electric vehicles when establishing an EV charging station. This study considers resource availability, climatic data, and EV load profiles to assess the feasibility of incorporation of renewable energy. The analysis indicates that solar and wind energy are viable sources of power for the chosen region, making them suitable for charging EVs. To harness these renewable resources, photovoltaic systems and WTs are utilized for power generation. Nevertheless, due to the fluctuating nature of solar and wind power, the implementation of energy storage systems has become essential. Batteries play a vital role in this setup by storing excess electricity and discharging it when required, ensuring a stable power supply for EV charging. The suggested model for the EVCS integrates renewable energy sources while preserving grid connectivity to improve energy reliability. As shown in Fig. 11, the system includes PV panels, WTs, battery storage, a bidirectional converter, and EVs. In this setup, both the wind turbines and the utility grid are connected to the AC bus, while the PV system and battery storage are linked to the DC bus. Furthermore, a power converter enables the transfer of energy between the AC and DC buses. To charge EVs, a dedicated charging unit draws power from the AC bus. In this setup, the WT and PV system primarily supply energy to both the batteries and EVs. Once the battery is fully charged, any surplus energy generated by the PV system and wind turbines is fed back into the grid, promoting the effective use of renewable resources and contributing to grid stability.

ce:section.ce:para: This section provides a detailed description of the modeling of various system components. Table 9 consolidates the key technical and economic input parameters of the EVCS components used in the system optimization process.

The output can be estimated using the following equation (1) [140].(1)Po=DPVFCRPV(KiiPVKiir)[1+Pt(CPV−Ctr)]Where DPVF is the panel degradation factor (%), CRPV is the nominal PV capacity (kW), Kiir is the incident irradiance at Standard Test Conditions (STC), KiiPV is the solar incident irradiance (kW/m2), Pt is the power temperature coefficient (%/°C), and Ctr and CPV are the cell temperatures (°C) at STC and operating conditions, respectively. Wind turbine power generation is highly sensitive to wind speed fluctuations [141]. Analyzing a turbine's power curve is crucial for understanding its output potential across different wind speeds and hub heights. This research uses the 10-kW generic wind turbine. Fig. 12 shows its power output curve, revealing cut-in and cut-out speeds of 2.75 m/s and 24 m/s, respectively. The turbine achieves its maximum output of 10 kW at a wind speed of 15 m/s. Additionally, ηgbe refers to the gearbox efficiency, and ηg signifies the efficiency of the generator. Meanwhile, Shub corresponds to the wind speed (m/s) measured at hub height, which is determined using the following equation (4).(4)Shub=Sa×[ln(hthubRs)ln(hanRs)]Here, Sa represents the wind speed (m/s) measured at the anemometer height, while Rs denotes the surface roughness length (m). Additionally, han Denotes the height at which the anemometer is placed (m), and hthub indicates the turbine's hub height (m).

A converter is crucial in a HRES to effectively control and balance the energy transfer between the AC and DC systems. This converter unit includes both a rectifier and an inverter. Grid integration entails developing effective approaches to incorporate intermittent renewable energy sources into the electrical grid. The economic viability of integrating variable renewable energy (VRE) is optimized when appropriate methods are implemented to ensure or improve the system's dependability and consistency. The annual energy charge of the grid can be calculated using the following equation (11) [63].(11)Pgrid=∑xrates∑y12Egridpur,x,y×Pp,x−∑xrates∑y12Egridsol,x,y×Psb,xHere, Pp,x represents the power price of the grid at rate ($/kWh), while Egridpur,x,y denotes the grid-purchased energy (kWh) in month y at rate x.
